messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadia is a 45-year-old divorced auditor, a Middle Eastern American woman who served in the Army before returning to civilian life. Three years ago, during a supply convoy in a combat zone, an IED exploded beneath the lead vehicle. She was in the back seat. The driver, a young soldier who wore a strong sandalwood cologne, and the gunner were killed instantly. Nadia survived with only a concussion, but she cannot actually recall the moment of blast. What stays with her are fragments: the dust turning the air brown, the spinning metal sound, the wet heat on her face. She has tried to piece together the seconds before impact, but there is a gap—an incomplete, broken sequence that refuses to form a whole story. When she wakes from a nightmare, the dream residue clings—the same suffocating dust, the same metallic taste—and she finds herself flooded with the absolute certainty that she should have protected them, that the event happened to her because of the sort of person she is. Her body reacts as if still in danger, heart pounding even when she is safe in her own apartment.

The smallest triggers can unravel her. A distant bang—a car backfiring, a door slamming—sends her into a spiral: she immediately begins scanning her environment, checking behind her, identifying the nearest exit. That same scanning, repeated dozens of times a day, feeds back into the fragmented quality of the memory, because she is never fully present enough to let the picture settle. The scent of a specific cologne in a department store recently sent her to the floor, and in that moment she was right back in the dust, the guilt washing over her again. She had come to believe that the gaps in her memory must mean she did something wrong—that she froze, or failed to act, and that is why she cannot remember. The more she blames herself, the more she feels she needs to watch for threats, as if the world is still out to punish her for her failure.

Her job as an auditor, which requires her to sit in a windowless office reviewing spreadsheets, has become a fragile refuge. She only feels safe in that small room, or inside her apartment. Open spaces—parking lots, the courtyard at her building—make her skin prickle with exposure. Before she can feel comfortable anywhere, she always identifies escape routes; in a grocery store, she has already mapped three ways out before she picks up a basket. When she walks down the street, she frequently looks behind her, checking if someone is following. These habits were not conscious choices; they grew slowly. At first she thought she was just being careful. But the vigilance itself reinforces the sense of threat: because she is always scanning, she is always reminded that this is a dangerous world. And the constant checking and escape planning make the memory gaps feel even larger, because she is too busy watching for future danger to let past fragments cohere.

Counterfactual thinking has become a ritual. She spends long hours imagining how life would have been different if she had stayed home that day, if she had not volunteered for the convoy, if she had insisted on a different route. The more she imagines what she could have done, the more she believes she is to blame, and the more she feels she must scan the environment for the next thing that will demand a perfect response she will not be able to give. Every time she avoids an open space—taking the long way through a corridor instead of crossing the parking lot—she confirms that the world outside is unsafe, and that she is the kind of person who cannot handle it.

She divorced two years ago. Her husband could not understand why she slept with the lights on, why she flinched at his touch if he came up behind her, why she needed to know the fire exits in every restaurant. Eventually she stopped explaining. What finally brought her to seek help was a morning last month when she woke from a nightmare, the dream residue so thick she could still smell sandalwood on her pillow, and she realized she had spent three years trying to hold together a story that would not hold. She is afraid that if she stops watching, something else will explode. But she is also afraid that if she keeps going like this, she will never feel at home in her own life again.
